sentence: Lansoprazole is a proton pump inhibitor, a medicine that lowers stomach acid, used for indigestion, heartburn, reflux disease and stomach ulcers.
note: NHS About: lowers stomach acid; prescribed for indigestion, heartburn, reflux disease, stomach ulcers; PPI class stated in NHS common questions/leaflet.

sentence: It is available on prescription only, and longer-term use is reviewed by a doctor because it is linked to low magnesium, vitamin B12 deficiency, bone fractures and gut infections.
note: NHS About: prescription only. NHS common questions: more than 1 year raises chance of fractures, gut infections, B12 deficiency; low magnesium after more than 3 months; doctor regularly reviews.

sentence: Indigestion and heartburn
note: NHS About lists indigestion and heartburn.

sentence: Reflux disease, where stomach acid flows back up towards the gullet
note: NHS About lists reflux disease; the explanatory clause is a plain gloss.

sentence: Stomach ulcers
Occasionally, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
note: NHS About: occasionally used for Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

sentence: Lansoprazole belongs to a group of medicines called proton pump inhibitors.
note: NHS common questions and emc leaflet describe it as a proton pump inhibitor.

sentence: It dampens down the enzymes in the lining of the stomach that make acid, so less acid is produced.
note: NHS common questions on how it works.

sentence: Having less acid is what eases symptoms such as indigestion, heartburn and reflux.
note: Joins NHS statements that it lowers stomach acid and is used for these symptoms; plain inference.

sentence: Symptoms usually start to improve within 2 to 3 days, although the full effect can take up to 4 weeks.
note: NHS: improvement within 2-3 days, full effect up to 4 weeks (from search summary of NHS pages).

sentence: Headache, which usually eases after the first week
note: NHS side effects: headaches usually ease after the first week.

sentence: Feeling sick, diarrhoea, stomach pain and constipation
An itchy or mild rash, dizziness or tiredness, and a dry mouth
Common side effects are usually mild and tend to go away when the medicine is stopped
note: NHS side effects: usually mild, go away when you stop.

sentence: Worsening stomach pain, yellowing of the skin or whites of the eyes, or dark urine can signal inflammation of the pancreas or liver and needs a same-day call to the GP or NHS 111
note: NHS serious side effects (rare, under 1 in 1,000). Route-to-care wording (GP or NHS 111 the same day) follows the NHS page's advice to contact a doctor or 111; exact route inferred.

sentence: Joint pain together with a red rash on sun-exposed skin can signal a skin form of lupus and needs a same-day call to the GP or NHS 111
note: NHS serious side effects: subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus. Route-to-care wording (GP or NHS 111 the same day) follows the NHS page's advice to contact a doctor or 111; exact route inferred.

sentence: Severe or persistent diarrhoea can signal an inflamed bowel and needs a same-day call to the GP or NHS 111
note: NHS serious side effects. Route-to-care wording (GP or NHS 111 the same day) follows the NHS page's advice to contact a doctor or 111; exact route inferred.

sentence: A serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is rare; swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, fast or difficult breathing, a tight throat, trouble swallowing, blue, grey or pale skin, sudden confusion or fainting needs a 999 call

Low blood magnesium is possible after more than 3 months of use and can cause tiredness, dizziness, muscle twitches or an irregular heartbeat, which calls for a GP appointment or NHS 111 if it happens
note: NHS common questions: low magnesium after more than 3 months; symptom list from search summary. Route of care inferred.

sentence: Use for more than a year may raise the chance of bone fractures, gut infections and vitamin B12 deficiency
Most adults and children can take lansoprazole, but the NHS advises checking with a doctor first in liver problems, pregnancy, trying for a baby, breastfeeding, low vitamin B12 or before an endoscopy
note: NHS Who can and cannot take (via search summary).

sentence: Lansoprazole may hide some of the problems an endoscopy would usually find
note: NHS Who can and cannot take.

sentence: It is not used by people who are allergic to lansoprazole or any ingredient in the product
People with osteoporosis or taking corticosteroids are advised to tell their doctor, because proton pump inhibitors have been linked to fractures of the wrist, hip and spine
note: emc leaflet says tell doctor; MedlinePlus notes fracture link.

sentence: Antacids can reduce how much lansoprazole the body takes in, so the pharmacist or doctor advises on timing
note: NHS other medicines: antacids reduce absorption; timing detail deliberately omitted.

sentence: St John's wort is best avoided because it may stop lansoprazole working as well as it should
Medicines that can interact include digoxin, itraconazole, ketoconazole, posaconazole, methotrexate, HIV medicines, rifampicin, warfarin, fluvoxamine, tacrolimus and theophylline
note: Lists from NHS other-medicines page and emc SmPC (ketoconazole, theophylline from SmPC); blended in search summary, so attribution to both.

sentence: It can make the emergency contraceptive ellaOne less effective, while regular contraceptive pills are not affected unless vomiting or severe diarrhoea stops the pill working
Alcohol is not ruled out, but too much increases stomach acid and can make symptoms worse
In pregnancy the NHS says omeprazole is usually offered instead of lansoprazole
note: NHS pregnancy page (search summary). The emc SmPC advises avoiding in pregnancy as a precaution; sources differ in wording.

sentence: While breastfeeding it can be taken, with attention to feeding problems, constipation, diarrhoea, vomiting or unsettled behaviour in the baby, and fertility does not appear to be affected
note: NHS pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility page.

sentence: Dizziness or tiredness can occur, so care is advised before driving or using machinery
A doctor regularly reviews whether continued treatment is still needed, particularly with long-term use.
note: NHS common questions: doctor regularly reviews ongoing use.

sentence: Clotting tests may be needed alongside warfarin, and blood levels of tacrolimus may be monitored when lansoprazole is started or stopped.
Lansoprazole is a medicine that lowers the amount of acid made in the stomach.
It is prescribed for indigestion, heartburn, reflux disease and stomach ulcers, and occasionally for Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
Reflux disease is the name for stomach acid repeatedly flowing back up into the gullet.
note: Plain gloss of reflux; widely accepted definition.

sentence: In the UK it is only available on prescription.
It comes as capsules that are swallowed and as orodispersible tablets that melt in the mouth.
note: NHS About: capsules and orodispersible tablets.

sentence: Local prescribing guidance describes the melting tablets as the choice for people who find swallowing difficult.
note: NHS formulary page (search summary): capsules by default, orodispersible tablets for swallowing difficulty; hospital/formulary source, not national.

sentence: Lansoprazole is a proton pump inhibitor.
It dampens down the enzymes in the lining of the stomach that make acid, so less acid is produced.
Symptoms usually start to improve within 2 to 3 days.
The full effect can take up to 4 weeks.
How long treatment lasts is decided by the prescriber and depends on the reason it was started.
note: NHS: doctor regularly reviews whether treatment should continue; wording generalised.

sentence: The NHS lists headache, feeling sick, diarrhoea, stomach pain, constipation, an itchy or mild rash, dizziness or tiredness, and a dry mouth as common side effects.
They are usually mild and tend to go away when the medicine is stopped.
Headaches usually ease after the first week.
Serious side effects are rare, affecting fewer than 1 in 1,000 people according to the NHS.
Worsening stomach pain, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or dark urine can signal inflammation of the pancreas or liver.
Joint pain with a red rash on sun-exposed skin can signal a skin form of lupus.
Severe or persistent diarrhoea can signal an inflamed bowel.
Any of these needs a same-day call to the GP or NHS 111.
note: Route-to-care wording (GP or NHS 111 the same day) follows the NHS page's advice to contact a doctor or 111; exact route inferred.

sentence: A serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is rare.
Swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, fast or difficult breathing, a tight throat, trouble swallowing, blue, grey or pale skin, sudden confusion or fainting needs a 999 call straight away.
Antacids can reduce how much lansoprazole the body takes in, so a pharmacist or doctor advises on timing.
St John's wort is best avoided because it may stop lansoprazole working as well as it should.
Medicines that can interact include digoxin, itraconazole, ketoconazole, posaconazole, methotrexate, HIV medicines, rifampicin, warfarin, fluvoxamine, tacrolimus and theophylline.
note: NHS other medicines page and emc SmPC.

sentence: The NHS says there is not enough information to say that other complementary medicines and herbal remedies are fine to take with it.
Alcohol is not ruled out, but too much increases stomach acid and can make symptoms worse.
Regular contraceptive pills are not affected, although vomiting or severe diarrhoea can stop a pill working.
Lansoprazole can make the emergency contraceptive ellaOne less effective, so another option may be suggested.

Most adults and children can take lansoprazole, but the NHS advises checking with a doctor first in liver problems, pregnancy, trying for a baby, breastfeeding, low vitamin B12 or before an endoscopy.
note: NHS Who can and cannot take.

sentence: Lansoprazole may hide some of the problems an endoscopy would usually find.

People with osteoporosis or taking corticosteroids are advised to tell their doctor.
In pregnancy the NHS says omeprazole is usually offered instead of lansoprazole.

sentence: While breastfeeding it can be taken, with attention to feeding problems, constipation, diarrhoea, vomiting or unsettled behaviour in the baby.
Taking lansoprazole for more than a year may raise the chance of bone fractures, gut infections and vitamin B12 deficiency.

For this reason a doctor regularly reviews whether treatment should continue.

The full effect can take up to 4 weeks, so it can take time to judge whether it is helping.

Anyone wondering about stopping after long use can ask the prescriber or pharmacist.
note: Signposting; the NHS says a doctor reviews ongoing use.
